02-01.summary: Opens the Research chapter by framing research as the highest-leverage part of SEO: pick the wrong keyword and you can waste years building a product nobody searches for. Chapter splits into fundamentals, research for new projects, and research for existing projects.
key_takeaways: Research is the most important phase — it determines whether the whole effort is worthwhile.
Choosing a low-volume or hyper-competitive keyword wastes years of work.
The chapter covers SEO fundamentals, finding/validating new niches, and competitor-driven research for existing sites.

02-02.summary: A brief setup lesson stating the fundamentals to cover before research: types of keywords, user intent, and match-and-exceed. Flags that three keyword types matter most in practice.
key_takeaways: Fundamentals to master first: keyword types, user intent, and match-and-exceed.
Of many keyword types, three are the most useful for real research (short-tail, long-tail, LSI).

02-03.summary: Explains short-tail vs long-tail keywords. Short-tail head terms have high volume but high competition and low supply; long-tails have low volume each but low competition (often KD under 20) and high supply, so a cluster of them can equal a head term's traffic with realistic ranking odds.
key_takeaways: Short-tail = high volume, high competition, scarce → home-page/brand target, long game.
Long-tail = low volume each, low competition (KD often <20), abundant → where new sites actually rank.
Roughly a dozen long-tails can match one short-tail's traffic, but with far better odds.
Short-tail terms usually live inside their long-tail variants.

02-04.summary: Covers LSI (semantically related) keywords — synonyms and related phrases for your main term. Generate them via an LLM or Ahrefs, re-measure volume/KD across the synonym set to find hidden goldmines, then pick one main keyword and weave the LSI variants through the content so Google ranks the page for all of them.
key_takeaways: List every synonym/related phrase for your main keyword (ask GPT; Ahrefs also surfaces them).
A low-KD synonym can have far more volume than the obvious head term (e.g. DP maker vs PFP maker).
Choose one main keyword, then mention LSI variants in the content for full topical coverage.
LSI expansion reveals the true size of an opportunity beyond a single term.

02-05.summary: Breaks down the four search intents and the content each demands: informational (how-to/what-is → articles), commercial (best/vs/review → comparison/curation pages), transactional (buy/download/tools → landing pages, convert now), and navigational (branded → ignore). Misreading intent wastes the click.
key_takeaways: Match content type to intent; never send a transactional searcher to a blog post.
Informational → articles/guides; commercial → comparisons/top-10s; transactional → landing pages/tools.
Many generator/maker queries are effectively transactional even without 'buy'.
Ignore navigational/branded keywords in research; the live SERP is the final intent arbiter.

02-06.summary: Introduces match-and-exceed: read Google's top 3 to learn the content format it rewards (its 'appetite'), match that format, then assess whether you can exceed the incumbents' quality. Low KD alone isn't permission — weak top results (thin tools, Pinterest, low page authority) are green lights; strong, well-linked incumbents are not.
key_takeaways: The top-3 content type tells you what to build; build the same format, not a blog post if they're tools.
Always ask 'can I make better content than this?' even when KD is low.
Pinterest/Wikipedia/thin sites ranking = easy to exceed with richer content + a free tool.
Strong, content-heavy, heavily-linked incumbents need authority you may not have yet.

02-07.summary: Defines the four decision metrics and their thresholds: Keyword Difficulty (target <20, ~10 backlinks to rank), Domain vs Page Authority (page authority/URL rating is the real bar; authority is logarithmic), Search Volume (skip <100, discount <500; click curve ~30/15/10% for positions 1/2/3), and CPC (monetization filter — high volume + ~$0 CPC = worthless traffic).
key_takeaways: KD <20 → rankable as a new site in ~1-2 months with ~10 backlinks.
Volume <100 = skip; <500 = discount; apply the 30/15/10% click curve to size real clicks.
Page authority (URL rating / links to the URL) matters more than domain authority.
High volume + low/zero CPC = nobody monetizes it; high volume + solid CPC + low KD = priority.

02-08.summary: Tooling guidance: all SEO tools buy from the same data brokers, so numbers are largely identical and the difference is UI/UX. Recommends picking one paid tool (Ahrefs, SEMrush, or cheaper Mongools); the course uses Ahrefs. Free tools (Keyword Planner, Answer The Public) are mostly lead magnets and insufficient.
key_takeaways: Keyword data is the same across paid tools — choose on UI/UX.
Course standardizes on Ahrefs; cheapest tier (~$29/mo) suffices for one project.
Pay for a tool if serious; free tools won't give the depth research needs.
If a user already pays for SEMrush/Mongools, map panel names rather than switch.

02-09.summary: Demonstrates the data-dump hunt for new niches: open Ahrefs Keyword Explorer, filter KD<20, volume>100, country US, then add a buildable 'include' word (generator/maker/free/AI) to surface low-KD high-volume tool opportunities. Browse for buildable gems and write them down — illustrated by finding AI tattoo generator (KD ~9, 20k searches).
key_takeaways: Empty Keyword Explorer + filters (KD<20, vol>100, US, include 'generator'/'AI') = a list of buildable niches.
Filter by transactional/commercial intent where you intend to monetize.
Most of the list is junk; you're mining for one or two buildable gems.
AI as a modifier finds fresh niches where KD is still low.

02-10.summary: Validates a candidate keyword through a gauntlet: confirm low KD, that searchers want something you can build, that they pay (CPC/paid competitors), solid volume/geography, a beatable live SERP, and — critically — size the whole cluster via Keyword Ideas and Also Ranks For. AI tattoo generator's 19k head term implied an 80k+ cluster and hundreds of thousands across tattoo ideas/styles/near-me.
key_takeaways: Validate the cluster (Keyword Ideas + Also Ranks For), not just the head term.
Confirm buildability, willingness to pay (CPC/competitors), and a beatable SERP.
A head term at ~19k can imply 80k+ across related terms — that's the real prize.
Also Ranks For reveals adjacent category directions (ideas, styles, locations) for a content site.

02-11.summary: Competitor research for the validated niche: open each ranking site in Ahrefs Site Explorer and compare domain vs page authority (URL rating) — a high-DA site often has a weakly-linked top page (~16 links, URL rating ~7) that's beatable. Then mine each competitor's Organic Keywords to harvest LSI variants (creator, designs, designer, maker) you missed.
key_takeaways: Page authority (URL rating / referring domains to the URL) decides winnability, not domain authority.
Top-3 pages with few backlinks are beatable with modest links + better content.
Mine competitors' Organic Keywords for LSI/keyword expansion; ignore their branded terms.
Newer (AI-era) modifiers stay low-KD because incumbents rank for older terms.

02-12.summary: Turns the validated keyword cluster into a website sitemap: home page targets the main short-tail keyword (built as a better free tool with added text), category/hub pages cover each keyword group (tattoo ideas, styles, artists), and long-tail keywords get programmatic SEO pages — all internally linked back to the converting tool, with loved features paywalled to monetize.
key_takeaways: Home page = one short-tail, commercial main keyword that contains the broad category term.
One category/hub page per keyword direction; long-tails handled via programmatic SEO.
Every sub-page links up to and upsells the home-page tool.
Ship the tool free, then paywall the most-used features; add text to thin tool pages for ranking/dwell.

02-13.summary: Teaches when to abandon a niche, with two failure modes: too little demand (head term has some volume but an empty surrounding cluster, near-zero CPC, no buyers — e.g. ComfyUI workflows) and too much competition (huge volume but KD in the 80s, only elite sites rank — e.g. car insurance). For too-hard niches, optionally hunt low-KD sub-niches but verify page authority.
key_takeaways: Empty cluster around the head term + low CPC = the market voting no; skip it.
Don't build a 'startup bet' on a near-empty niche when you need traffic now.
KD in the 50s-80s with high-DA incumbents = unwinnable for a new site.
In too-hard niches, mine sub-niches but re-check page authority before committing.

02-14.summary: Starts research for existing businesses: find the top competitor for your main keyword, load their Organic Keywords in Ahrefs Site Explorer, and list terms you don't rank for. The cheapest wins come from adding a missing phrase to an existing page, since Google often doesn't equate synonyms (PFP vs DP, picture vs photo).
key_takeaways: Reverse-engineer the top competitor's Organic Keywords to find terms you're missing.
Quickest win: add a missing keyword/phrase to an existing page.
Google doesn't always merge synonyms — add the variant explicitly (e.g. DP pic).
Prioritize low/zero-KD terms with real volume that you don't yet rank for.

02-15.summary: Uses Ahrefs Top Pages to find pages a competitor built that you didn't think of: open a high-traffic page's overview to see its keywords, spot whole new page angles (a crypto laser-eyes page, a funny-PFP page) on low-KD terms, and exploit competitor keyword cannibalization. Build the missing page, make it better, and upsell your main product from it.
key_takeaways: Top Pages reveals new page concepts, not just keywords.
Build the missing page (often a quick tool/variant), exceed it, and upsell your core product.
Spot competitor keyword cannibalization (multiple pages on one term) as an opening.
Keep one focused page per main keyword; create new pages for secondary keywords.

02-16.summary: Covers Ahrefs Content Gap (competitive analysis): enter your domain plus competitors to automatically surface keywords where they rank in the top and you don't. Triage out the too-hard terms, then drill into promising gaps with Keyword Ideas/Also Ranks For. This automated method complements — but doesn't replace — the manual Top Pages dig.
key_takeaways: Content Gap automatically lists keywords competitors rank for that you don't.
Filter out high-KD/high-authority terms; keep realistic gaps.
Drill into promising gaps with deeper keyword research before committing.
Run both automated (Content Gap) and manual (Top Pages) gap-finding — HeadshotPro was found this way.

02-17.summary: The Also Ranks For rabbit hole for existing sites: put your main keyword in Keyword Explorer, open Also Ranks For, filter to ~500+ volume and strip branded/non-commercial terms, then keep going deeper to surface long-tail and regional variants (DP for Instagram in Asia vs PFP in the West). Related terms are easy for your site to rank for.
key_takeaways: Also Ranks For surfaces related terms your site is well-positioned to rank for.
Filter to ~500+ volume; remove branded and non-commercial terms.
Descend the rabbit hole repeatedly to find long-tail and regional variants.
Regional naming differs (DP vs PFP) — target the high-volume regional variant.
